title: Bioinformatics 101
text:
Linux is often used to analyse large amounts of data. Whenever the data comes from a biological source, we call this type of analysis bioinformatics. There are a number of common files that are used in many different types of analysis. We have seen two of them so far, FASTQ and BED.
Many of the most common types of file that you will have to work with as a bioinformatician take the form of structured text files, examples include:

Standard formats for representing raw sequences

FASTA
FASTQ

Tabular formats for representing aligned reads or genome features

BED
GTF
SAM


These standard file formats have specific structures. This ensures that information is always recorded in the same way and provides compatibility with bioinformatics software and tools.

title: Bioinformatics 101
text:
Tools
Today, we will look at a fairly typical bioinformatics task; aligning reads to an existing reference genome. To simplify things, the following choices about the analysis have been made:

We will skip any pre-processing of reads, even though they might contain adapter sequences or low quality data.
STAR will be used for aligning reads, this is a very popular aligner for RNA-seq data. Many different tools are available, but most of the tools will produce SAM files as outputs.
The samtools package will be used to view and summarise the resulting SAM files. Again other toolkits are available, however samtools is a very popular and commonly used tool.
Finally, we will use bedtools to look at reads mapping to gene regions of the reference genome.

By default, these tools are not installed on Linux servers and have to be installed separately.
Note: This is not a full pipeline, we will provide examples of more thorough sequencing analyses in future workshops.

title: Bioinformatics 101
text:
Analysis
First, lets take a look at the data. We are going to align RNA-seq reads from saccharomyces cerevisiae to the yeast reference genome. The files are in the yeast_files directory.
cd ~/Intro_to_Linux/yeast_files/
The reference genome sequence is stored in yeast_genome.fasta, while gene annotations and locations are recorded in yeast_genes.bed.


 Challenge 1:

Print the first 5 lines for each of the reference genome files.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

To get the first 5 lines of a file, we can use the head command.
head -n 5 yeast_genome.fasta

head -n 5 yeast_genes.bed



The first column of the BED file refers to the chromosome name, and in the FASTA file the name behind the > symbol refers to the name of the chromosome. As you can see, there is a discrepancy between the files and the names for the chromosome.
This is a common problem in bioinformatics, as data can come from different sources and use different naming conventions. We need to fix this problem before we move on. The easiest fix is to remove chr from the BED file. For this, the sed command can be used, which can replace patterns in a file with another piece of text. For example:
sed "s/^chr//" yeast_genes.bed > yeast_genes_fixed.bed
Let’s break down the sed command:

s stands for search and replace

The pattern between the first two / is the text we want to search for
The text between the second and third / is the replacement text

Thus s/^chr// will find lines that begin with “chr” and remove these three characters.

The results are written to yeast_genes_fixed.bed. Note that sed does not edit the original file yeast_genes.bed. Inline editing is possible with -i option in sed.
To confirm the replacement has worked, lets run the head command again.
head -n 5 yeast_genes_fixed.bed
This only confirms it for the first few lines. To check throughout the file, we can pipe a few useful commands together.

cut can extract columns of data from a file
sort provides classic character and numerical sort functionality
uniq removes consecutive lines that are duplicated

cut -f 1 yeast_genes_fixed.bed | sort | uniq
The command above will thus show us the unique values in the first column of yeast_genes_fixed.bed.


 Challenge 2:

See if you can produce a count for the number of genes per chromosome. Hint: take a look at the uniq command, it has an option to count values


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

uniq --help
The uniq command has an option -c. If we add that to the command, it should give us a count of the number of lines (genes) for each chromosome.
cut -f 1 yeast_genes_fixed.bed | sort | uniq -c



Now that our genome annotation files are compatible, we can proceed with aligning RNA-seq reads to the reference. The first step is to index the genome. Indexing is used by mappers to make mapping faster and easier. Most alignment tools have the option to create an index. The command to create an index for STAR is below:
## Create a folder for the index
mkdir star_index

## Run STAR in genomeGenerate mode
STAR --runThreadN 5 --runMode genomeGenerate --genomeDir star_index --genomeFastaFiles yeast_genome.fasta --genomeSAindexNbases 10
The --runThreadN option tells STAR how many ‘threads’ or ‘CPUs’ to use. Many command line tools can run on multiple CPUs to speed up processing. However, you should be wary of hogging all of the compute power on a shared server. We will look into how to determine the number of threads later.
The --genomeSAindexNbases option controls the size of the index created. You can read more about the various options available in the STAR documentation.
Once the index has been created, the reads can be mapped to the genome. The command requires paths to the raw reads and the index folder.
STAR --genomeDir star_index --readFilesIn raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz --runThreadN 2 --outFileNamePrefix raw_yeast_rnaseq_data. --outSAMtype BAM SortedByCoordinate --readFilesCommand 'gunzip -c' 
The --readFilesCommand 'gunzip -c' option instructs STAR to unzip the compressed fastq files.
The output is a BAM file, which is the binary version of a SAM file. It contains a lot of information about each read and its alignment to the genome.
We can use samtools flagstat to check how many reads map to the reference genome.
samtools flagstat raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.Aligned.sortedByCoord.out.bam
We can see that 100% of the reads map to the reference genome. Many of the reads have secondary locations, meaning that the read aligns to multiple locations on the genome. For RNA-seq data this is a normal occurrence.
The bedtools package has many tools for performing operations on genomic data. We can use genomecov to convert a BAM file into a bedgraph file of sequencing coverage. The output bedgraph file shows the sum of sequencig reads overlapping each genomic base.
bedtools genomecov -ibam raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.Aligned.sortedByCoord.out.bam -bg > raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.genomecov.bg

head raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.genomecov.bg
We can use intersect to count the number of reads overlapping each gene in yeast_genes_fixed.bed.
bedtools intersect -c -a yeast_genes_fixed.bed -b raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.Aligned.sortedByCoord.out.bam > raw_yeast_overlap_data.bed

head raw_yeast_overlap_data.bed
For each gene, the number of overlapping reads is recorded in the 7th column.


 Challenge 3:

What is the maximum amount of reads mapping to a gene?
Hint: Use the cut and sort commands, check the --help of sort to see how to sort numeric values.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Using cut we can extract the 7th column and then sort them by number.
sort --help

cut -f 7 raw_yeast_overlap_data.bed | sort -n 
The maximum count is 3,730 reads.





 Challenge 4:

Can you find which gene has the highest read count?
Hint: Use grep


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Using grep we can extract the exact number.
grep "3730" raw_yeast_overlap_data.bed
There are different lines that contain this number, but only one in the last column, which is for the gene “RDN37-2”.



Alternatively, sort allows you to sort a file by specific columns.
sort -k7,7nr raw_yeast_overlap_data.bed | head
We can break this down as follows:

-k7,7: Sort using the column range 7,7 (We could use multiple columns)
-n: Perform a numerical sort
-r: Perform a reverse sort to output the results in descending order

title: Bioinformatics 101
text:
Threads
Now, as mentioned, many of the commands run within bioinformatics can run on multiple threads (also referred to as cpus). Every computer has them, but processes need to share them. Which mean that if we are working on a server, we need to make sure that the commands being run aren’t claiming all the threads that are available.
To check how many processes are currently running, there are two commands to use:

top shows all active processes
htop gives a user friendly representation of the processes currently running along with CPU and memory usage on the server



 Challenge 5:

Using htop, can you see how many tasks are running?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

There should be a line which says how many tasks are currently running. The screen also shows how much memory is being used.



Before running any process, it is good to check what the status of the system is.

title: Bioinformatics 101
text:
AWK
Lastly, one powerful command line tool that can be very helpful, though somewhat complex, is awk. It can help analyse, filter or manipulate structured files. Lets look at an example to see if we can use awk to find the longest genes within our genome. Gene length isn’t captured within the BED file, however the start and stop position are given. The follow command will give us the top 10 longest genes.
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '{print $4,$3-$2}' yeast_genes_fixed.bed | sort -k2,2nr | head
Lets break down the command, because this is complex.

-F '\t' sets what the separator is within the file. This is the character which is between the columns. \t as we saw at regular expressions means tab.
-v OFS='\t' tells awk that the output should be tab separated as well
'{print $4,$3-$2}' is where the magic happens. awk processes every line of a file one by one. It separates the all the columns and renames them to $1, $2, etc to the last column index. This means we can make changes to the order, but also do calculations with the different columns. If we substract the start position of our gene from the stop position, it will give the gene length. What this means for this part of the command is that it will report the 4th column followed by the stop column minus the start column.
sort -k2,2nr will sort the resulting list. -k2,2 specifies the list should be sorted by the second column, and nr specifies that the sort is numeric and should be sorted in the reverse order.

If awk is of interest to you, take a look at Effective AWK Programming. Don’t worry if this looks extremely complex, this is an advanced Linux command that will become more useful as you get into more difficult challenges.

title: Working with Files
text:
So far, we have only worked with empty files and haven’t looked at the content of files. There are several core ways to look at the content of a file. First, lets move into the folder below.
cd ~/Intro_to_Linux/yeast_files/
The first file we will take a look at is a BED file. This file contains information on genes located on a reference genome, with each line representing a unique gene. This is a standard text file format used in bioinformatics. There are several ways to look at the content of text files. The first is head, which will print the first few lines of the file to the terminal.
head yeast_genes.bed
Similarl to looking at the start of the file, there is a command for looking at the end of a file, the command tail will return the last few lines of the file.
tail yeast_genes.bed
Both of these can be very useful to be able to peek at files, especially when they are really large. To look at the full file, the cat command can be used to print the whole file to the terminal.
cat yeast_genes.bed
For large files, the content will whizz past, too fast to read. To be able to scroll through the content of files easily the command less is useful.
less yeast_genes.bed
You can scroll through the BED file one line at a time using the [Down Arrow] and the [Up Arrow] keys. You can also use the [Page Down] or [Space] and [Page Up] or [B] keys to scroll through the file one page at a time. To access the help, use the [H] key and finally to exit the file, use the [Q] key.


Take a look at the --help for head. Print the first 5 lines of the BED file.


Solution


Solution. 

First, lets look at the help for head.
head --help
From the results, we can see that -n can be used to print a specific number of lines.
head -n 5 yeast_genes.bed



Another very useful command is wc (word count). This command will report the number of lines, words and bytes within the file.
wc yeast_genes.bed
Often it will be used to look at the number of lines within the file. To only get the line count, add the -l option.
wc -l yeast_genes.bed

title: Working with Files
text:
Searching
In many cases, looking at the full file might not be useful. A way to search for specific text is using grep. For example, we can look for specific genes in our annotation file.
grep "YAL040" yeast_genes.bed


 Key points

The grep command has a lot of different options, an overview of the most important options can be found below.

-i will make the search case insensitive
-v will report all lines that do not match the searched term
-c will count the lines with a match

There is also the option to use regular expressions within grep. If you have never heard of regular expressions, these are expressions that will help search for patterns instead of fixed text. Some characters can be used to search for patterns.

^ represents the start of a line
$ represents the end of a line

More complex regular expressions can be used in grep with the options -E and -P.

\t represents a tab
\n represents an enter (or new line)
. matches any single character
* represents zero or more occurrences of the character before the *
+ represents one or more occurrences of the character before the +

title: Working with Files
text:
Binary files
Binary files are non human readable files. These files are specifically for computers to read. This includes zip files. Generally, they are compressed to take up less space, which is great for large bioinformatics files. In the yeast folder, there is an example of a compressed file. The file is gzipped, which is a different form of zip file. FASTQ files are commonly gzipped. These files contain DNA sequence information from sequencing platforms. The files contain headers, sequences and quality information for each sequencing read. We will look more in depth into them later on, but for now we will focus on compression.
head raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz
Clearly not human readable. Sometimes we need to get information from these files without wanting to unpack them on the server. Linux has a number of commands that will work on compressed files. Similar to the commands we used previously, we can use zless, zcat and zgrep on compressed files.


 Challenge 1:

Extract all lines starting with an @ symbol from raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz and count the number of lines.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

First, lets get all the lines that start with an @ symbol. Because this is a binary file, we need to use zgrep. Remember that we want lines that start with the symbol, so we need to use ^
zgrep "^@" raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz
To get the count of lines that match this, we can use the -c option for zgrep.
zgrep -c "^@" raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz

title: Working with Files
text:
Zipping and Unzipping
Even though compressed files use less disk space, in some cases we want to unpack them. There are 3 main types of compression files that need different ways of unpacking: zip, gzip and tar.

unzip can unpack zipped files, zip can create zips. Zips can contains single files or complete folders.
gunzip can unpack gzipped files and gzip created gzipped files. Generally gzip is used for single files.
tar can be used to unpack and create tar files. Tar is used for folders and often another form of compressing is used on top of it. You will often find tar.gz files.

The two main compression types found using Linux are gzip and tar. Lets look at an example for both.
gunzip raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz


 Challenge 2:

Check if the file is now unpacked by printing the first 20 lines of the file.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

We can use head to print the first lines of the file.
head -n 20 raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq



To gzip the file again, the command gzip is used.
gzip raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq
This should again results in a file with the same name, with an added .gz to the end.
ls


 Challenge 3:

Navigate back to the Intro_to_Linux folder, what is the name of the file which ends in tar.gz.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Use cd to move back to the Intro_to_Linux folder. Use ls to see an overview of the content.
cd ~/Intro_to_Linux

ls
There is a file in the folder named tar-latest.tar.gz.



To unpack the file, we can use tar. Several options are needed to unpack the file.

-x specifies that files need to be extracted.
-v reports what the command is doing (verbose).
-a automatically handles decompression (gunzip in this case)
-f (which needs to be at the end) specifies the tar file to unpack.

As you can see below, we can add all the options together into a single combination for the tar command. The command is the following:
tar -xvaf tar-latest.tar.gz
This will take a couple of minutes, if it is confusing to add options together, the previous is the same as the following:
tar -x -v -a -f tar-latest.tar.gz
As the file is unpacked, a list of files and folders is written to the terminal. We can double check that a folder named tar-1.35 has been created within the current folder using ls.

title: Command output
text:
So far, most of our command outputs have been printed to screen without saving the results or doing anything with the results. Here we will look at how to direct our outputs into a file.
To write the results of a command into a file, we can redirect the output with the > symbol. Rather than printing results to the terminal, this symbol will write to the filename given after the > symbol.
For example, let’s create a file named my_commands.txt that contains the text “My commands:”, followed by our command history.
We first need to add the line “My commands:” to a new file. This can be done using the echo command, which simply prints out the text that you give it.
echo "My commands:"
If instead, we redirect the output to a file then the text will be saved.
echo "My commands:" > my_commands.txt


Check if the file has been created and contains the redirected output.


Solution


Solution. 

Remember that we can use a cat or less to take a look at the content of a file.
cat my_commands.txt



Now that we have the header, we need to add the content of our command history. We can get our history using the history command. Using > we can redirect the output to our file.
history > my_commands.txt

head my_commands.txt
It seems that the file has been overwritten and the redirect has removed our original header. With redirects, Linux overwrites existing files without warning. Luckily, there is a way to append to an existing file without overwriting it, using >>.
echo "My commands:" > my_commands.txt

history >> my_commands.txt

head my_commands.txt
Now, the original content has been kept and the history of commands has been added to the file.


There are several different options to redirect output.

> redirects output, overwriting if a file exists
>> redirects output and appends the results to an existing file
2> will redirect errors only, overwriting if a file exists
2>> will redirect errors only and adding errors to an existing file
2>&1 redirects errors to the standard output (useful if you want to record errors and outputs together)

title: Command output
text:
Combining commands (pipes)
Some of the power of Linux comes from the ability to string commands together to form “pipelines”. Using the | pipe symbol, the output of one command can be used as the input for a second command.
For example, if we want to count the number of lines in a gzipped file, this can be done by first using zcat to get the uncompressed content of the file and piping the output into wc to count the lines and characters within the file:
cd ~/Intro_to_Linux/yeast_files/

zcat raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz | wc
If you simply run wc on the file, you will get a result, however it will be nonsense as wc doesn’t know how to decompress the file before counting the content.
Let’s say we want to find the first five lines in raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz that contains the sequence ACTG.
We could perform this in three separate commands and save the input as we go:
## Save the uncompressed output
zcat raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz > raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq

## Find all lines with ACTG
grep "ACTG" raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq > ACTG_raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.txt

## Print the first five lines
head -n 5 ACTG_raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.txt

## Remove intermediate files
rm raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq ACTG_raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.txt
Pipes are particularly as they remove the need to create these large intermediate files. They can also save time. In this example, there is no need to keep reading the input file once five instances of ACTG are found. When we pipe commands, all commands will terminate when the final command has completed. This can save considerable time with large files.
zcat raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz | grep "ACTG" | head -n 5

title: Command output
text:
Exercises
Below are a number of exercises exploring files and redirection.


 Exercise 1:

Go into the yeast_files folder. Save the first 20 lines of the raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz to a file named header.txt, without unpacking the gzipped file.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

The first thing we should do is extract the content of the gzipped file. With zcat we can print the whole file to the terminal, then pipe this into the head command to extract the first lines. Remember that we can change the number of lines we want with -n. And finally we can redirect the results into a file.
cd ~/Intro_to_Linux/yeast_files

zcat raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz | head -n 20 > header.txt





 Exercise 2:

Extract the lines starting with an @ from the gzipped file. Print the last 10 lines to screen.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

We can search within a gzipped file using zgrep. To search for lines starting with an @ we have to use the ^ symbol. Once we have these extracted, print the last 10 lines with tail. By default, it prints the last 10 lines.
zgrep "^@" raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz | tail





 Exercise 3:

Extract the lines starting with an @ from the gzipped file. Print the first and the last 10 lines to a file called names.txt.
NOTE: You can’t do this in a single command. You will need to get the first 10 lines and last 10 lines separately and combine them in a single output file.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

We can use >> to append the output of our second command to the output of our first command.
zgrep "^@" raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz | head > names.txt

zgrep "^@" raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz | tail >> names.txt

title: Text Editors
text:
Several command line text editors exist for creating and editing files.

Highly customisable and extensible:

emacs:
vim:

Beginner friendly:

nano:


Today we will briefly look at nano, which is simple to use and installed on all Linux distributions. Nano is specifically designed for editing plain text files, the staple input/output format used by most command line tools.
Command line text editors are not designed to take the place of feature rich graphical word processors for creating highly formatted documents (Microsoft Word, Google Docs etc). Instead, they are fast and versatile editors for command line programming.
Just typing nano will open a new blank file.
nano
Try typing some text into your editor. Specific options are shown at the bottom (run by holding CTRL + your chosen option).
To save your file use CTRL+O, it will then prompt you to name your file:
File Name to Write: myfile.txt
You can then exit with CTRL+X.


Check to see if the file has been created and what it contains.


Solution


Solution. 

ls
cat myfile.txt



We can also open a existing file with nano.
nano myfile.txt
If you edit this file and then try to exit without saving, it will prompt you with ‘Save modified buffer?’ Y/N before again clarifying output file name (Useful!).
Earlier, we created a file called my_commands.txt. Open this with nano and make some annotations (generally ‘#’ are used to denote comments) and clean up the file however you like.
nano my_commands.txt
Here, I’ve added a comment to remind me of an option (Note, your numbers on the left of command history will differ):
 2013  date
 # Using -u displays the date in UTC time
 2014  date -u
 2015  date --help
You can navigate with the arrow keys but the ‘Where Is’ CTRL+W function may be useful here.

We can also open a existing file with nano.
nano myfile.txt
If you edit this file and then try to exit without saving, it will prompt you with ‘Save modified buffer?’ Y/N before again clarifying output file name (Useful!).

nano my_commands.txt
Here, I’ve added a comment to remind me of an option (Note, your numbers on the left of command history will differ):
 2013  date
 # Using -u displays the date in UTC time
 2014  date -u
 2015  date --help
You can navigate with the arrow keys but the ‘Where Is’ CTRL+W function may be useful here.

title: Getting started with the Shell
text:
One of the first questions people often ask is: Why do I need Linux? If people are familiar with graphical interfaces used for programs in Windows, why do bioinformaticians use command line? The short answer is that command line and Linux are lightweight, highly flexible, and maybe most importantly for research: free. Besides this, many bioinformatics tools are written and used without a graphical interface, which keeps them lightweight. This makes command line knowledge essential for bioinformatic data processing.
Like Windows and macOS, Linux is an operating system. It manages the computer’s hardware and allows you to run applications. There are many different versions (or distributions) of Linux. Some commercial distributions have a paid licence, but many are completely free. One of the most popular choices is Ubuntu, which is free to download, easy to install, and widely used by both beginners and experienced users. It is the also the version of Linux installed on the DRP-HCB servers.
One thing to note is that bioinformaticians are not the only people who use Linux. Linux powers a large proportion of the world’s servers, supercomputers, and cloud computing infrastructure. Many of these systems do not have a graphical user interface. Instead, they are controlled through the command line. By avoiding the overhead of a graphical interface, more memory and processing power are available for running computationally intensive tasks, such as analysing genomic data.

title: Getting started with the Shell
text:
Bash Shell
If many Linux servers do not have a graphical user interface, how do we interact with them? The answer is through the command line. If you have ever used Command Prompt or PowerShell on Windows, the basic idea is very similar. Instead of clicking buttons and navigating menus, you only use the keyboard, you type commands to tell the computer what you want it to do.
Linux has a specific vocabulary for how to ask for things, it contains a large collection of built-in commands that allow you to perform almost any task. These commands let you navigate through directories, create and edit files, move or copy data, install software, and run programs. While there are many different Linux distributions, the vast majority use the same core commands, so the skills you learn on one distribution are generally transferable to others. Occasionally, there are small differences, but these are usually minor.
The environment in which you type and execute these commands is called a shell. The shell acts as an interpreter between you and the operating system: it reads the command you type, executes it, and displays the results. At first, using the command line can feel unfamiliar because there are no buttons or menus to guide you. Instead, you communicate with the computer using commands and options, much like learning a new language. Throughout this course, you will gradually learn the most useful commands and develop the confidence to navigate the Linux operating system efficiently.

title: Getting started with the Shell
text:
Connecting
Today, you will connect to one of the DRP-HCB servers to start your Linux journey. Connecting to the server is dependent on the machine you are working with. To connect:

Both Linux and Mac have a “Terminal”, which is command line and can connect to a server using ssh. By typing in the following in your terminal, you can easily connect to the DRP server.
Replace <UUN> by your own UUN or username.

For Windows, a tool like MobaXTerm needs to be installed to be able to connect to a server easily. Connecting uses ssh in this case as well. Take a look at the MobaXTerm demo to learn how to connect using ssh. Make sure to use you UUN as your username and the server link as follows:

bifx-core1.bio.ed.ac.uk
You might be asked if you trust the server, make sure to answer yes. Once you’ve entered your password you should connect to the server and see something like the following:
Welcome to Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (GNU/Linux 6.8.0-117-generic x86_64)

 * Documentation:  https://help.ubuntu.com
 * Management:     https://landscape.canonical.com
 * Support:        https://ubuntu.com/pro

and constitutes an offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
If you are not authorised to use this system, terminate this 
session now.

All activity on this system is monitored and recorded.

Please direct any queries to IS.Helpline@ed.ac.uk.

This prompt shows that you are logged in to the bifx-core1 bioinformatics server, and that you are in your home directory (which is referred to using the ~ character on Linux systems).

title: Getting started with the Shell
text:
Commands
The basic structure of most Linux command is as followed:
command [option(s)] [argument(s)]

command: the operation or program you want Linux to execute
options (also called flags or switches): modify the way the command works
arguments: filenames or other targets that direct the action of the command

Options and arguments are not always needed for commands to run. If no options or arguments are given, default settings will be used. You can run commands by typing in the command and pressing ENTER.
Here is an example of using default behaviour with the date command.
date
The command results in the date being displayed in BST (British Summer Time). However, if you use the -u option:
Note: be aware to put a space between the command and the option.
date -u
The date will be displayed in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time). By using options, you can change the default behavior of a command.
How do you know what options are available to a command?


 Challenge 1:

Try using different single letter options with the date command. Can you find an option that doesn’t exist? What happens?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Run date with -p (date -p), you should get an error telling you what you are doing is invalid.

title: Getting started with the Shell
text:
Help
While the use of options and arguments makes commands more powerful and flexible, they can be difficult to remember, and can vary between different versions of the command. Luckily, there are several ways to find out what a command does and what options are available for a command. Most commands can be used with the --help or -h option, which will provide a description of the command and the options.
date --help
In some cases, commands will not have the --help or -h option. In these cases, man or info pages might be available. The man command displays the manual page for a command, while info provides more detailed information. Below is an example of how to use man.
man date
To get out of the information screen, press q for quit.


 Challenge 2:

Run the command:

date -d '25 Dec' +%j
Using the help options, can you explain what this command has done?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Looking at the result of the command, you can already see that this gives a number. Look at the %j option in the help documentation of date, it explains that %j gives the number of the day of the year. The 25th of December is the 359th day of the year (unless it is a leap year, then it is the 360th day).

title: Getting started with the Shell
text:
Command line tips

History
When working on the command line, you often want to scroll through or rerun previous commands. Using the ↑ and ↓ keys, you can explore and rerun without having to write the whole command again. The history command can also be used to print or search all of our recent commands.


Tab completion
Using tab completion allows you to type part of a command or filename and press the Tab key. The shell will try to complete the text based on available commands and filenames.
For example, if you want to run the date command, you can type dat and press Tab to complete the command. This works, because the date command is the only available command that starts with dat.
If you type da and press Tab, the shell will not complete the command, because there are multiple commands that start with da. In this case, hit the Tab key twice to see the available options.


Shortcuts
There are a few keyboard shortcuts within our shell that will come in handy whenever you are working within this environment.


 Key points


Ctrl+a or Home will move the caret (or text cursor) to the beginning of the line
Ctrl+e or End will move the caret to the end of the line
Ctrl+k will cut text from the current position of the caret to the end of the line
Ctrl+y or the middle mouse button will paste the last selected text at the caret position
Ctrl+l will clear the terminal

Be aware that Ctrl+c, which is normally used for copying selected text, will terminate any command that you are currently running. If you want to copy something from the terminal, use the right mouse button to copy.

title: Creating Files
text:
To be able to work within Linux, we need to learn to make, move and delete folders and files. To start, lets make sure that we start in the Intro_to_Linux folder.
cd ~/Intro_to_Linux/
First, we will take a look at creating directories. For this we can use the mkdir (make directory) command. Let’s start by creating two folders, temp1 and temp2
mkdir temp1 temp2
As you can see, we can create two folders in one go. The mkdir command can take multiple names and will create all the names separated by a space in the current directory, unless specifically told to make it somewhere else. Lets check if the directories have indeed been created.
ls


Move into the temp1 directory.


Solution


Solution. 

Remember to use cd for this.
cd temp1



There are several ways to create files. The quickest way is to use touch, which will create empty files.
touch myfile1.txt myfile2.txt
Again, multiple files can be created at the same time if we provide multiple names separated with a space.
ls
Files can be copied to other directories using the cp (copy) command.
cp myfile1.txt ~/Intro_to_Linux/temp2/


Check if there is a file named myfile1.txt in the temp2 folder


Solution


Solution. 

Remember to use ls for this.
ls ../temp2



Because the file was copied, the current directory should still contain the file as well.
ls 
Files can be moved using the mv (move) command. Similar to the copy command it takes the file which is to be moved and the location to which it should be moved.
mv myfile2.txt ~/Intro_to_Linux/temp2/


Check if there is a file named myfile2.txt in the temp1 and in the temp2 folder


Solution


Solution. 

Remember to use ls for this.
ls 

ls ../temp2



Because the file was moved, it should no longer be in temp1 but only in the temp2 folder.
Move can also be used to rename files, for that we give it the current name and the name it should be renamed to.
mv myfile1.txt myfile1_renamed.txt 
And of course double check if the file has correctly been renamed.
ls
NOTE: Use the mv command with caution. Linux does not check if the filename you are moving to already exists. Any existing files will be overwritten. The -i option to mv provides an interactive version of move which asks before overwriting existing files.
Go back to the Intro_to_Linux directory:
cd ~/Intro_to_Linux
The last thing to look at in this chapter is how to remove files and folders. Both can be deleted using the rm command, however for folders an option needs to be added. To remove files, we can do the following.
rm temp1/myfile1_renamed.txt
If the same thing is done for a folder, an error is reported.
rm temp1
Because it is a folder, rm needs to know that we are okay with removing a folder and everything that is inside of it. Even if the folder is empty, rm needs confirmation.
rm -r temp1


Linux doesn’t always reply to commands. For Linux, no news is good news. If we do not get any reply from Linux after running a command, this means that the previous command has been done and there is nothing to report. If we want to make sure commands are run correctly, we need to do checks ourselves.
In some cases, the option -v can be added to commands to have a verbose output which reports what the command is doing.



Remove folder temp2. Make sure to use the -v option while removing the folder.


Solution


Solution. 

We have to combine multiple options for this.
rm -r -v temp2





Whenever you remove or overwrite files from the command line, they are gone. Forever. There is no Trash or Recycle Bin like within a graphical environment. There is no easy way to get them back!
Some servers have daily backups, however this is not something to depend on. Make sure you have backups of important data.
One tip is to always do an ls of the folder you want to remove before actually deleting it. This way you can make sure you are removing the correct folder and are aware of what is inside the folder. You can also use the -i interactive option, this will ask you to confirm everything it removes. Be very aware of typos and spaces in your commands!
## EXAMPLE - DO NOT RUN
#rm -r ~/Project /temp2
Instead of removing ~/Project/temp2 folder, the command above will attempt to remove the full Project folder and temp2 in the root folder, because of the space in the directory name. This could be catastrophic.

title: Creating Files
text:
Permissions
So far, we have worked within our home directories on the server. By default, this folder is owned by you. When we want to share files and folders with other users, we can change ownership of files or change permissions to allow others to access.
Each file (and directory) has three sets of permissions:

user: Permissions for a user that owns the file or directory
group: Permissions for a user group associated with the file or directory. A user may belong to several groups but a file or directory only has one group.
others: Permissions for anyone else that is not the owner or part of the associated group.

Each file and directory also has three basic permission settings:

read (r): Ability to read the content of a file or directory.
write (w): Ability to write or edit a file or directory.
execute (x): Ability to run the file as a program. For a directory, this is the ability to go into the directory and access files inside.

For a directory with only execute permissions, you can read the contents but only if you already know the names of the files. You cannot list the files without the read permission on a directory. This is rarely useful, generally on any directory you want to set read and execute permissions both on, or both off.
To take a look at this, lets create a file again.
touch myfile.txt
To get information on permissions, we can use the ls command again. To list permissions, the option -l needs to be used.
ls -l myfile.txt
The first column (-rw-r–r–) contains the permissions.

The - at the start indicates that this is a file. If it was a d, it would be a directory. If it was an l it would be a link (we will talk about links later on).
The next 3 characters are user permissions. rw- means that the user can read the file (r), can write to and edit the file (w), but cannot execute the file (-).
The next 3 letters are group permissions. r-- means that the group can read the file but cannot edit or execute the file.
The last 3 characters are others permissions. Again we see r--, which means others can see the file but make no changes or execute the file.



 Challenge 5:

Look at the permissions for all the files in the Intro_to_Linux folder. Identify different permissions over the different files.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

First we have to list the details for all the files and directories using ls
ls -l



To change permissions of files, the chmod (change mode) command can be used.

The chmod command uses the letters u, g and o to represent user, group and others.
To change permissions for everyone you can use a for all.
The chmod command uses the letters r, w and x to represent read, write and execute.

For example, to stop other users on the system from accessing myfile.txt, we can remove the permissions for group and others:
chmod g-r myfile.txt

chmod o-r myfile.txt

ls -l myfile.txt
If we want to add permissions, use a + instead of a -.

Setting permissions recursively (directory and all files inside of it) is possible, for this the -R option can be used. The command below is a very handy command. It means “make my current directory and everything inside of it readable and writable by me”. Note the uppercase X properly sets the directory permissions, remembering that we want both read and execute set on directories. If we used a lowercase x it would also make all the files executable, which we probably don’t want.
chmod -R u+rwX .
File permissions can be confusing, here is a useful tool to help.

title: Creating Files
text:
Symbolic links
Sometimes, we want to easily access a file in another directory without copying it into our working directory. Symbolic links, also known as soft links or symlinks, are pseudo-files that link to another file or directory (similar to a shortcut in Windows). In bioinformatics, these links are often used to reduce duplication of large data files or reference genomes.
Symbolic links are created using the ln (link) command with option -s. The -r option makes the command behave more nicely, similar to the cp or mv command.
ln -sr ~/Intro_to_Linux/genomes/human/hg38/genome.fa ./


 Challenge 6:

Check if the link is created and what the permissions are for the link.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Using ls we can look at the files to check if the file is there and using -l we can see the permission details.
ls -l



Deleting symbolic links does not remove the original file. If, however, the target file to which the link points is moved or deleted, the link will stop working.

title: Bioinformatics on the Linux command line
text:
Welcome to our introductory Linux command line workshop.
During this course you will learn to:

Connect to a server
Navigate the file system using the Linux command shell
Use basic shell commands to view and filter data
Perform basic analysis with bioinformatics tools

This course is hosted by the Bioinformatics Core at the Discovery Research Platform for Hidden Cell Biology.

title: Exploring the Filesystem
text:
Before we get to work with Linux, it is good to know how the system is structured. Files on Linux are grouped into directories (also called folders, similar to Windows and Mac). The directories are structured in a tree structure. This means directories are within other directories, creating a complex hierarchical tree like structure. At the base of it all is the root directory, which is indicated with “/”. This directory holds everything. It can contain files and subdirectories. Each subdirectory in turn can contain other files and subdirectories, and those can contain files and subdirectories, and so on.
An example of the file system is shown below.
User directories are usually stored in the /home directory and named after each user. UUN in the figure below should be replaced with your own UUN to find your own home directory.





It is vital to understand that you always work within a specific directory and any commands you run will be run in the context of that specific directory.
There are a few special characters, when working within the file system, that refer to specific folders. The table below gives an overview of the special characters that can be used to browse the tree.



Character
Meaning




/
root directory


~
home directory


.
current directory


..
parent directory



With the knowledge of what the tree looks like and the use of special characters, we should be able to find our files. To identify any file or directory we need to determine its path. The path is the route to the file or directory starting from a directory. Paths are written as the list of directory names separated by a forward slash.
For example /home/johndoe/mouse_genome.fa links to a file named mouse_genome in the home folder belonging to johndoe. When referring to files starting from the root directory, we call these paths absolute paths. This means that no matter where you are in the filesystem, the path will always refer to the same file.
We can also use relative paths, which are paths that start from the current working directory. For example, if we are currently in the home directory of user johndoe, we can refer to the same file simply as mouse_genome.fa. Relative paths are generally shorter and easier to type, but they are dependent on the current working directory.
A user logged in as janedoe would have a different home directory under /home/janedoe, and the relative path mouse_genome.fa would only work if they also had a file named mouse_genome.fa in their home directory. Still, they would be working with a different file from johndoe. To access the same file as johndoe, janedoe would need to use the absolute path /home/johndoe/mouse_genome.fa, or a relative path ../johndoe/mouse_genome.fa.
If you are ever in doubt, use the absolute path (start the path from the root).


There are several best practices for choosing good file and directory names.

Everthing in Linux is case sensitive. If in doubt, stick to lower case.
The filename myfile is not the same as MyFile, Myfile, or myFile. This is also the case for any commands we work with.
File and directory names should only contain letters, numbers, hyphens, underscores and full stops
File and directory names should not contain any spaces

In contrast to graphical environments, the command line interface can become cumbersome whenever our file or directory names contain spaces or special characters. For example, the shell will consider my file to be two files, i.e. “my” and “file”. If you have files containing spaces or special characters and you want to use them within Linux, you will need to enclose the full filename in quotation marks or you will need to escape spaces and special characters with a backslash. This makes sure that the shell understands it is part of the filename: "my file" or my\ file
To make our life easier, it is best to avoid spaces and unusual characters all together.

Whenever we first start a shell on a Linux system, your working or current directory will be your home directory. On most Linux systems your home directory will be called /home/username.
Unless we reference the path, Linux will look for a file in the current working directory. If we ever want to check what the current working directory is, we can use the command pwd which stands for present working directory.
pwd


What is your current working directory?


Solution


Solution. 

Run pwd, and look at which directory you are in. Check if your username is your UUN.

title: Exploring the Filesystem
text:
Before we get to work with Linux, it is good to know how the system is structured. Files on Linux are grouped into directories (also called folders, similar to Windows and Mac). The directories are structured in a tree structure. This means directories are within other directories, creating a complex hierarchical tree like structure. At the base of it all is the root directory, which is indicated with “/”. This directory holds everything. It can contain files and subdirectories. Each subdirectory in turn can contain other files and subdirectories, and those can contain files and subdirectories, and so on.
An example of the file system is shown below.
User directories are usually stored in the /home directory and named after each user. UUN in the figure below should be replaced with your own UUN to find your own home directory.





It is vital to understand that you always work within a specific directory and any commands you run will be run in the context of that specific directory.
There are a few special characters, when working within the file system, that refer to specific folders. The table below gives an overview of the special characters that can be used to browse the tree.



Character
Meaning




/
root directory


~
home directory


.
current directory


..
parent directory



With the knowledge of what the tree looks like and the use of special characters, we should be able to find our files. To identify any file or directory we need to determine its path. The path is the route to the file or directory starting from a directory. Paths are written as the list of directory names separated by a forward slash.
For example /home/johndoe/mouse_genome.fa links to a file named mouse_genome in the home folder belonging to johndoe. When referring to files starting from the root directory, we call these paths absolute paths. This means that no matter where you are in the filesystem, the path will always refer to the same file.
We can also use relative paths, which are paths that start from the current working directory. For example, if we are currently in the home directory of user johndoe, we can refer to the same file simply as mouse_genome.fa. Relative paths are generally shorter and easier to type, but they are dependent on the current working directory.
A user logged in as janedoe would have a different home directory under /home/janedoe, and the relative path mouse_genome.fa would only work if they also had a file named mouse_genome.fa in their home directory. Still, they would be working with a different file from johndoe. To access the same file as johndoe, janedoe would need to use the absolute path /home/johndoe/mouse_genome.fa, or a relative path ../johndoe/mouse_genome.fa.
If you are ever in doubt, use the absolute path (start the path from the root).


There are several best practices for choosing good file and directory names.

Everthing in Linux is case sensitive. If in doubt, stick to lower case.
The filename myfile is not the same as MyFile, Myfile, or myFile. This is also the case for any commands we work with.
File and directory names should only contain letters, numbers, hyphens, underscores and full stops
File and directory names should not contain any spaces

In contrast to graphical environments, the command line interface can become cumbersome whenever our file or directory names contain spaces or special characters. For example, the shell will consider my file to be two files, i.e. “my” and “file”. If you have files containing spaces or special characters and you want to use them within Linux, you will need to enclose the full filename in quotation marks or you will need to escape spaces and special characters with a backslash. This makes sure that the shell understands it is part of the filename: "my file" or my\ file
To make our life easier, it is best to avoid spaces and unusual characters all together.

Whenever we first start a shell on a Linux system, your working or current directory will be your home directory. On most Linux systems your home directory will be called /home/username.
Unless we reference the path, Linux will look for a file in the current working directory. If we ever want to check what the current working directory is, we can use the command pwd which stands for present working directory.
pwd


What is your current working directory?


Solution


Solution. 

Run pwd, and look at which directory you are in. Check if your username is your UUN.

title: Exploring the Filesystem
text:
Files and Folders
We are going to play with files and directories and take a look at how to browse them and refer to them. To look at which files and subdirectories we have within our folder, we can use the ls (list) command.
ls
It might be that there are currently no files within your directory. Just to have some files to play with, we will copy them from a central location on the DRP-HCB Bioinformatics server. For this we will use the cp (copy) command.
cp -r /library/training/Intro_to_Linux ./
NOTE: if you are working from your own server or system, download the data as followed and unpack it. You do NOT need to run the following if you are working on the DRP-HCB Bioinformatics server. Don’t worry about the messages you get on screen, we will talk about these later on.
wget https://bifx-core3.bio.ed.ac.uk/~hdeweer/Intro_to_Linux.tar.gz
tar -xzvf Intro_to_Linux.tar.gz
If we take a look again at what is in our folders, we will now see that a folder has been added called Intro_to_Linux.
ls
If we want to know what is inside the folder, we can use ls again and use an argument to specify the folder that we want to explore.
ls Intro_to_Linux
The folder is in our home directory, which means the ls command has run in the current location. We can use absolute paths as well.
Replace <UUN> by your own UUN or username.
ls /home/<UUN>/Intro_to_Linux
We can also use the ~ shortcut to reference our home directory.
ls ~/Intro_to_Linux
The last 3 commands all have the same results, which should show us the content of the folder Intro_to_Linux.
As mentioned before, Linux has difficulties with spaces in names. There is one directory in our Intro_to_Linux directory that contains spaces. When Linux reports files or directories that contain special characters, it will put quotes around the name to indicate there is something about the name which is outside the general rules. Before we get into how to deal with files and directories with spaces, lets look at how to navigate the system.

title: Exploring the Filesystem
text:
Navigaton
We aren’t limited to staying and working in one directory. To move between directories, use the cd (change directory) command and add the folder that you want to navigate to as an argument.
cd Intro_to_Linux
If you take a look at the actual prompt, this has now changed to reflect your current location:
<UUN>@bifx-core1:~$ to <UUN>@bifx-core1:~/Intro_to_Linux$


 Challenge 2:

Navigate back to the parent directory of this folder. Confirm the folder you are in is your home folder.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Remember the different special character meanings in the table above. Using .. we can navigate to the parent directory. We can use pwd to check which folder we are currently in.
cd ..
pwd
If you used a different method to get back to your home folder, that is amazing, there are multiple ways to get back to your home folder e.g.
cd ~
cd /home/UUN



Using .. we can go to the parent directory of the current directory. We can use this multiple times to go up several levels.
cd ../..
pwd
Notice that when we ask for the pwd we just get a /. This means we are now be in the root directory and have therefore gone up two levels.


 Challenge 3:

Navigate back to the Intro_to_Linux folder.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Looking at the ls commands above we showed 3 different ways to get to the folder. Use any of these to get back to your home.
cd ~/Intro_to_Linux





 Challenge 4:

Navigate into the Intro_to_Linux/genomes/human folder.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

From where we are currently, we don’t have to use the full path, we can use a relative path.
cd genomes/human



Because we are already in the Intro_to_Linux folder, we can create a relative path from our current folder into the folder we actually want to be in. It is important to remember that relative paths change whenever our current working directory changes. Absolute paths will always be the same. But what happens if we try to navigate to a folder that exists but is not in the current directory?
cd mouse
The computer tells us that the directory does not exists.


 Challenge 5:

Navigate to the Intro_to_Linux/genomes/mouse folder using a relative path.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

If we want to navigate to the mouse folder using a relative path from our current working directory, we need to know where we are (we can always double check this is pwd). Knowing that we are in the Intro_to_Linux/genomes/human folder and wanting to go to the Intro_to_Linux/genomes/mouse folder, we can use the .. character to go up a level.
cd ../mouse



We know how to navigate normal directories, but what about the strange one we saw previously with the spaces in it. Lets go back to the Intro_to_Linux folder first.
cd ~/Intro_to_Linux
Within this folder there is a folder named “dir with spaces”. If we want to know what is inside this folder, we would use the ls command with the name of the folder behind it. What happens if we do just that?
ls dir with spaces
Basically, Linux thinks we want to know what is inside 3 different folders: dir, with, and spaces. None of these exist and so we get errors. When using ls, Linux puts quotes around the name when it reports it to us, if we want to ask what is inside we can use the same system.
ls 'dir with spaces'


 Challenge 6:

What happens if we try to use Tab completion?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Type the first part of the folder name “dir” and press Tab. The following should show up.
ls dir\ with\ spaces/



To complete the command, Linux puts a \ before the spaces. This is known as escaping characters. When we put a \ before a special character, we tell the computer to disregard its normal meaning. We can also use that in full paths.
ls ~/Intro_to_Linux/dir\ with\ spaces
It’s not the nicest, but it does mean we can look at files that have special characters without having to rename them before working with them.

title: Exploring the Filesystem
text:
Exercises
Below are a number of exercises designed to explore the filesystem.


 Exercise 1:

Navigate back to your home directory. List the contents of the Intro_to_Linux directory without moving into it.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

We do not have to move folders to be able to see the content of a folder. Using ls we can specify the folder we want to look at.
cd ~

ls Intro_to_Linux





 Exercise 2:

Navigate to the Intro_to_Linux directory.
List the contents of your home folder without moving directory.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

We do not have to move folders to be able to see the content of a folder. Using ls we can specify which folder we want to look at.
cd Intro_to_Linux

ls ../





 Exercise 3:

Using --help, learn how the options -a and -l affect the ls command.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Run ls with the --help option. Take a look at -a.
ls --help
If we use the -a option when running ls, we do not ignore entries starting with ..
A good folder to try this on is the home folder.
ls ~

ls -a ~
Do you see the differences in files reported? Files beginning with . are known as hidden files. These are generally configuration files or files used by the operating system.
If we use the -l option when running ls, the output is in long mode. This gives extra information about files and folders, like their size, access permissions and when they were last modified.
ls -l ~





 Exercise 4:

List the contents of the genomes folder within the Intro_to_Linux folder using its absolute path.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Remember that the absolute path starts from the root /
Replace the  with your UUN.
ls /home/<UUN>/Intro_to_Linux/genomes





 Exercise 5:

Write the relative path in two different ways from you current location for the genomes folder within the Intro_to_Linux folder.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Because we should currently be in the Intro_to_Linux folder, the following should work.
ls ~/Intro_to_Linux/genomes

ls genomes

title: Installing Software
text:
One of the essential things in bioinformatics is the ability to install tools. On the server, often installation is limited to admins only. Sometimes this can take a long time or when testing new tools, we don’t want to disturb the admins. Thankfully, there is a solution to be able to easily install tools in your home. Conda and mamba are two managers that are essential to get to know, both are part of miniforge.
Conda and mamba are often used to install tools within something called environments. This means that multiple tools can be installed within your home folder without interfering with other tools. Tools in bioinformatics have very different requirements which will clash, using environments we can still install multiple tools on the same machine with ease. Below is a short guide on how to install miniforge, create an environment and install tools.

First, miniforge needs to be downloaded. To get online files to our machines easily, wget can be used.
wget https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
If you want to use mamba instead, install micromamba. All the other commands will be the same, just replace conda with mamba
Once the file has been downloaded, the installation can begin.
bash ./Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
The licensing will be printed on screen, you can scroll on using space or enter. Make sure to accept the license and then set the location for installation. By default it installs in your home folder, generally this is a good place to install miniforge. The installation itself will take a few minutes. At the end of the installation, miniforge will ask if you want to initiate. Yes means that everytime you start a shell connection, miniforge will be active. No means you need to activate it yourself. To activate, run the following:
source ~/miniforge3/bin/activate
To check if miniforge is active, (base) will be added to the start of your command line. Once this is active, conda can be used to create an environment. As an example, we will create an environment and install STAR into it. The following will create an environment:
conda create -n STAR
We need to accept that the environment is being created. To activate the new environment:
conda activate STAR
The start of our command line should now change to (STAR). Lets actually install STAR:
conda install STAR
Accept the installation. Once finished, this mean that STAR is installed without interfering with any other tools or asking an admin to install it for us. As long as the environment is active, the command can be run.

We can double check this is now installed in our home by using type. This will tell were the installation location of a tool is.
type STAR
Finally, to deactivate the environment:
conda deactivate
Whenever needed, you can install tools in your home. Tools can be installed together, especially if they need to be run together. However, the more tools installed, the more likely you tun into installation issues.

If ever you need to check which environments you have installed, a list can be created.
conda env list
Further information and best practices for managing tools on these servers can be found here
